chapter_theme: First songs at Kanchipuram (காஞ்சீபுரம், 1 of 3): in dense rhythms the poet asks to stand beyond the tattvas and the quarrels of the sects, confesses flattering patrons, the prison of the body, old age and his own worthlessness, and asks for the feet and a poet's speech; the praise dwells unusually long on the Goddess of Kanchi, who did penance by the Kampa and keeps the thirty-two charities, and on Siva and Vishnu worshipping Murugan at Kachi.
structure_note: A short opening song (308) that ends at the six shrines rather than Kachi; then songs in a heavy four-line rhythm (309 to 320) whose second halves often praise the Goddess (313 to 315, 317, 318) or the myths of Siva and Vishnu (309, 310, 312, 316, 319); two songs in another metre (321, 322) share the closing line on the lord of Thirukkottam.

308.reading: A short song: the poet asks that base birth not come near him, that he become Murugan's servant, and that he be given the grace of jnana so that his deeds end, with a compassion that takes away his shame. The praise names Murugan who excels in gift and penance, the companion of an excellent consort, the young one who gave the sacred padhigams, and the lord who grows in the six holy shrines.
308.nuance: ஆன திருப்பதிகம் அருள் இளையோனே: 'the young one who gave the holy padhigams' identifies Murugan with Sambandar, the child poet of the Thevaram padhigams. சாரதி உத்தமி துணைவ is unclear: சாரதி may name the Goddess or a consort, and the line may be divided otherwise. நாணம் அகற்றிய கருணை could also be the compassion that ended Valli's shyness.

309.reading: The poet praises Murugan as the one who, for the parrot of the hunters' forest, melted, went and bowed at her feet and swooned in infatuation, and the one who ends the sorrow of pure devotees, and asks that, worshipping him so with desire quenched and singing his fame, he be looked on and made to stand beyond the end where the Vedas' rows of devotion, the turiya state and all the tattvas vanish. The praise tells of Daksha's sacrifice, where the god of the discus and Brahma were struck in fear, the sun's teeth knocked out, the bird's wings cut and the guardians' army scattered, after Daksha's daughter, keeping her vow, entered the fire; Siva, who raged that day, worships Murugan at Kachi.
309.nuance: The plea reverses the usual roles: the first half gives Murugan's own infatuation (மயற்கொண்டு அயர்பவன்) for Valli, and asks for the poet's desire to be quenched (இச்சை தணித்து). துரியமும் தப்பித் தத்வம் அனைத்தும் தொலையும் அந்தத்துக்கு அப்புறம்: the goal is beyond turiya and the tattvas, as in 203. The sacrifice is named by its details: Daksha (தக்கன்), his daughter in the fire, the sun's teeth, the wings cut off the bird (குயில், here perhaps Agni in bird form).

310.reading: The poet confesses that, though he learned the poetry that worships Murugan of the golden arms and the red vel that reduced the mango in the sea to dust, he went to the people of the world, fawned on them, called a man a kalpaka tree for his giving, the sinless one, a Kumanan who gives whatever is wished, and, blind with begging, stole all the words of meaning and strung them to suit; he asks whether this confusion will not clear. The praise names Rama, who for Janaka's daughter of matchless chastity burned the whole kin of Lanka and cut the ten crowned heads with a single arrow, and names the sun, Indra, Sukra, the moon, the guardians, Agastya, Brahma, Vasishtha, the Vedas, the pure devotees whose action has ceased, and Siva himself as worshipping Murugan at Kachi.
310.nuance: The confession is the poet's trade again: the patron is flattered as the wishing tree and as குமணன், the Sangam chieftain famed for giving. இரவான குருடு, 'the blindness that is begging', and சத்தம் அனைத்தும் திருடி, stealing every word, make the flattery a theft from the poetry owed to the Lord. The long list of worshippers at Kachi ends with those whose action has ceased (செயலொழிந்து).

311.reading: The poet calls the body a stinking frame of bones and blood bound with nerves, a prison of karmic bonds, a raft whirling in the dark-waved sea of birth's sorrow, a hollow dwelling of the instruments that carries the filth of death and stumbles in all eight directions, and asks to escape the crowd of sects who learn the world and shout themselves weary and to reach the quality of staying within, at one. The praise names Murugan whom the three-eyed Goddess, wishing tree of chastity, delights in, the guru whose feet Siva worships, he who gives siddhi to devotees reciting the syllables daily, and the one whose heart melts for Valli's hands, waist, hair, lips and breasts, worshipped by the gods at Kachi.
311.nuance: The body images pile up as in 30: frame (சட்டம்), prison (சிறை), raft in the sea of birth (செனன ... துக்கக்கடல் ... தெப்பம்), hollow house (பொக்கப் புக்கில்). The remedy is not only escape from the body but from the sects that 'learn and shout and tire' (கற்றுக் கத்தி இளைக்கும் சமய சங்கம்). எட்டக்கரம் may be eight syllables or a misdivision; it is left unexplained.

312.reading: The poet strings Murugan's names, the one who threw the sakti at the golden Krauncha, knocked Brahma on the head and fettered his hands, the god whom Siva loves, the one whose hand Ganesa held, the patron who spoke his desire to the young parrot of the millet field, and asks whether, having learned these names, his clinging will go and he will gain the one meaning hidden in every thing. The praise tells of Ravana, who fought the eight elephants of the quarters and pulled up golden Kailasa by its roots, then had his twenty arms crushed under one toe, and of Siva who afterwards gave him a sword; Murugan stands at Kachi, having that god and his consort, Kailasa and the southern hill of the true guru.
312.nuance: பசை ஒழிந்து ... பொருள் தொறும் பொத்தப்பட்டது ஒர் அத்தம்: the plea is for the meaning enclosed in every object once attachment has gone, a pervasion read through the names. Brahma knocked and fettered (குட்டிக் கைத்தளையிட்டு) is the Om story, though Om is not named here. தெற்குச் சற்குரு வெற்பு, the southern hill of the true guru, is Swamimalai.

313.reading: The poet confesses that he has no great poetry of devotion to worship Murugan as the child of Ganga who freed the imprisoned gods, that his mind was never purified, that he learned many tattvas only to fall into argument, and that he has not gained the high vow by which those who reach the supreme state stand rapt and free of all attachment; he asks how else his sorrow can go. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess, Siva's consort with the trident and cane bow, Bhadra, the great thing unknown to anyone, the lotus-handed creeper, whose child Murugan is, and of the sakti that split the mountain touching Brahma's egg, at Kachi.
313.nuance: பரவசம் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பரவ்ரதம்: the devotee's rapture is what frees from attachment, not learning; தத்வம் பலவையும் கற்றுத் தர்க்க ம(த)த்துவம் sets learned argument against it. Much of the litany of the Goddess is hard to divide.

314.reading: The poet asks to see the meaning the devotees praise as Murugan, the common ground that holds all the ninety-six tattvas yet stands free of them, the truth hard to know for the six sects who argue and quarrel in anger every day, and, having seen it, to sing his deeds and teach it in every direction; he asks for the small anklets and golden lotus feet. The praise lists Ganesa's offerings, sesame, puffed rice, appam, fruit, roots, cane, sugar, gram and pittu, names him the elephant-faced brother, and names their mother Gauri, who bore the old universe and rescues worshippers from the waves of birth, at the side of the naked Siva, at Kachi.
314.nuance: எண்பத்தெட்டு எட்டு இயல் தத்வம்: eighty-eight and eight, the ninety-six tattvas of the Saiva count. சகலமும் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பொது: the Lord holds all and clings to none, the formula used again in 320; பொது, 'the common', makes him what all the quarrelling sects share. The plea ends in teaching (திசைதொறும் கற்பிக்கை), a rare missionary note.

315.reading: The poet names Murugan Saravana of the fierce sakti, the thief who hides in the mind, the lord of the cock, the lord of the serpent hill, of Palani, of Kachi and of Vanji, and asks whether, singing him so in Tamil with flawless love, forbearance growing, pride left, his own qualities ended and having reached the quality that has no other, free of all attachment, he will not get even a little grace to attain the guru's feet where pure devotees abide. The praise is of the Goddess, worn at Siva's side with his crescent, karandai, serpent, datura, skull and konrai, Tripura, Durga, Sakti, the pure green-hued woman, whose son gives siddhi to his servants.
315.nuance: சித்தத்துக்குள் ஒளிக்கும் கரவடன், 'the thief who hides in the mind', is a bold epithet for the indwelling Lord. குணம் அடங்கக் கெட்டு குணம் அற்று ஒன்று இலதான குணம் அடைந்து: the goal is a quality beyond the qualities. குருபதம் is both the guru's feet and the guru's state.

316.reading: The poet asks for the ripeness to reach the state attained when the mind's action ceases, through a love that opens as he learns of Murugan's hills, his vel that split the peak and his arms, and through the clear knowledge that sees the world, where delusion grows like an anthill, as a bubble; he names Murugan the god who told his father what he lacked, who cuts the fear of devotees, at Kachi. The praise tells of Vishnu, the dwarf who became greater than all while Sukra trembled, and the man-lion who tore out the entrails of Hiranya when the little boy Prahlada spoke the truth, the Murari who sleeps on the serpent with the discus, father of the world, whom Murugan grants siddhi.
316.nuance: ப்ரபஞ்சத்தைப் புற்புதம் ஒக்கும்படி நாடும் அறிவு: the world seen as a bubble. பக்வம், ripeness, is the soul's readiness for grace. அத்தற்கு அற்றது செப்பும் கடவுள, 'the god who told his father what he lacked', points to the teaching of Siva. The Vamana and Narasimha stories are named by their details (குறியவன், சுக்ரன், சிறுபாலன் குதலை, கனகன்). The last lines on who receives siddhi are unclear.

317.reading: The poet asks whether, thinking of the lotus of the sakti that fought, while Vishnu and Brahma showered flowers, the gods worshipped and a crore of ghosts danced to the drums on the battlefield where the Asuras were pierced, and praising Saravana the beautiful one of Kachi, he will reach the boon of service in his mind. The praise is a long picture of the Goddess's body, her sandal-dressed breasts, slender waist, a voice holding the notes kaikkilai, tuttam and kural, the navel that bore the worlds, cloud-dark hair, tilak and pearl-hung neck, and her compassion that gives siddhi to devotees: Murugan is the son of Gauri Amba and lord of all.
317.nuance: The first half is almost all battle, sung in drum syllables, with the plea folded into its last line (சித்தத்துக்கு வரத் தொண்டு அடைவேனோ). The Goddess's voice is described with the names of the Tamil musical notes (கைக்கிளை, துத்தம், குரல்).

318.reading: Not a plea but thanks: the poet calls himself one who never spoke even in dream of Murugan's mango of Kachi, the serpent hill, Palani, the southern hill of the true guru, Kathirai and Thiruchendur, who stole all that suits this body and whirled in fancies, who never melted and worshipped him as the jewel in Amba's hand, the new pearl of old Ganga and the treasure of the destitute, and asks what words could compare with the forbearance by which Murugan bore his faults and placed him among devotees. The praise names the Goddess of southern Kachi, sweeter than candy, mother of all worlds, the young woman who did penance in the waters of the Kampa, took the measures of grain and nurtures the thirty-two charities, and Murugan who told the truth to her consort.
318.nuance: பிழையுடன் பட்டுப் பத்தருள் வைக்கும் பொறை: the forbearance here is the Lord's, who bears with the poet's faults. The Kanchi legend of the Goddess is told by its details: penance in the Kampa (கம்பையினூடே தவமுயன்று), the measure of grain (படி) and the thirty-two charities (அறம் இரண்டு எட்டு எட்டு எட்டு, read as a count). சத்யம் உரைக்கும், telling the truth to Siva, is the teaching of 6 and 12.

319.reading: The poet pictures himself old: the skin hanging loose on its frame, hair white as a crane, head and body worn, bones and joints slack, the senses changed, walking with a stick and staggering off course, a frail, half-mad old man whose teeth all fall, while others say 'chee chee', his descendants 'chi chi' and his own wife spits 'thu thu'; before that despised birth, he asks to reach the lotus feet with anklets. The praise tells of Siva, who yoked the Veda horses with the reins, mounted the chariot with the sun for its wheel and burned the three cities with one arrow, worshipping Murugan at Kachi, and of the vel that struck Brahma, pierced the mountain and the sea and cut down the Asuras.
319.nuance: The scorn is given in sounds (செச்செச்செ, சிச்சிச்சி, துத்துத்து) set to the beat, the household's disgust heard rather than described. The poet asks for the feet before old age, not at the hour of death as in 28 or 68.

320.reading: The poet heaps names on himself: a mind of hatred and fault, without penance, wholly false, without refuge, a sinner standing in the rubbish of kin, without forbearance, empty of any bond to the one who holds all the tattvas and stands free of them, cruel, without the art of learning Murugan's boundless praise, block-witted, base, without a way; he asks whether he will reach Murugan by thinking even in dream of his arms, his vel, Kathirai, the golden hill and the other shrines and all of Kachi. The praise tells of the vel that made the roaring seas cry out, ended Surapadman's clan, eased the gods' distress so that Indra returned to his city, and saw Brahma punished, and of the feet with golden anklets.
320.nuance: The self-abuse (துரிசாளன், வெற்றன், கட்டைப் புத்தியன், மட்டன்) is a set piece, as in 29. Inside it is the formula of 314, the Lord who holds all and stands free (சகலமும் பற்றிப் பற்று அற நிற்கும் பொருள்): the poet's lack is that he has no bond to him.

321.reading: Before Death drives out and drags away alone the breath dwelling in this rag of a false body, a great hut that lets out urine and filth, built with limbs to hold all the deeds and given by a father and mother, the poet asks Murugan to come and gladly grant him the power to speak with love, in good and flawless words, of his fragrant red feet. The praise is of the Goddess: Siva who burned the three cities, and she who, frightened by the flooding river, embraced Kampar so that his body was marked, and who gives her feet to those who think of her lotus feet; Murugan is Gauri's son, lord of Indras at Thirukkottam.
321.nuance: சல மலம் விட்ட ... குடில் and தரவரு பொய்க்குள் கிடந்த கந்தல்: the body is a latrine-hut and a rag given by parents. The Kanchi legend of the Goddess embracing Ekambaresvara (கம்பர்) in the flood is named by its details. திருக்கொட்டம் is the Kamakottam of Kanchi. The battle lines on Sura taking many forms and the peacock are hard to divide.

322.reading: The poet asks for a birth in which, having sung great poems on the peacock, Murugan's arms, Valli and his red lotus feet with anklets, he will be honoured by many poets as a true poet, a master who knows the tattvas, a virtuous man of good qualities, and gain the golden feet; and whether the world's calling him forbearing and a renunciate who fears the false world will not bring him to the supreme consciousness. The praise is wholly of the Goddess: daughter of the mountain, whose womb bore the world, the Brahmin lady who keeps the thirty-two charities without lack, Sankari, Neeli, the peacock beauty who holds the poison in her throat, Digambari, 'our mother', Ambika, Tryambaki, Gauri: Murugan is lord of Indras at Thirukkottam.
322.nuance: An unusual plea: for fame as a poet and a name for virtue (புலவன் எனத் ... தலைவன் எனத் ... குண புருஷன் என), joined to release. புதுமை அல(ச்) சிற்பரம் பொருந்துகை may mean 'it is no wonder' or a 'new union with the supreme'. The thirty-two charities (முப்பத்திரண்டு அறம்) are here named outright, as in 318. Shares its closing line with 321.

links.note: Both confess the poet's begging trade, praising patrons as wishing trees and clouds; 310 adds the name of the Sangam giver Kumanan and calls the flattery a blind theft of the words owed to the Lord.
Tirumular says the Lord is not the thing the six sects hold; 314 makes him the truth hard for the six sects who quarrel daily, and yet the common ground (பொது) that holds all.

Both set the Lord who is one with everything yet apart against the confusion of the six sects; 257 mocks their images and wealth, 314 their angry argument, and asks to teach the truth in every direction.
Both see through the bubble: the Naladiyar's body is a bubble in the rain that forms and bursts, while 316 sees the whole world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) as a bubble, and asks for the ripeness to reach the Lord.

Both picture the old man with failing speech or senses, leaning on a stick, staggering, teeth gone; the Naladiyar's still has eyes for desire, while 319 adds the disgust of his kin and wife and asks for the feet before that day.
Both picture the poet's old age with stick, white hair and loose teeth while others mock; 68 asks Murugan to come at the hour of death, 319 to reach the feet before that despised birth.

source_issues: Song 308 is under the Kanchipuram heading but ends at the six shrines (ஆறு திருப்பதியில் வளர் பெருமாளே) and does not name Kachi.
Song 318: one corrupt character, in கம்பையினு஡டே (line 268), probably கம்பையினூடே.
Song 321: last line has இநதிரர், a typing slip for இந்திரர் (322 has the correct form).
